questions.question: 1. What is the time complexity of removing the root from a heap when the heap property must be restored afterward?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Although accessing the root is constant time, restoring the heap after removal may require moving an element down the heap.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A heap has logarithmic height, so restoration does not require scanning every element.
explanations.c: Correct. Removing the root and restoring the heap property takes $O(\log n)$ time because the adjustment follows a path whose length is bounded by the heap height.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A single root-removal operation does not require sorting the entire heap.

questions.question: 2. How many root-removal operations are required to remove all 10 elements from a heap if one element is removed at each operation?

explanations.a: Incorrect. One operation removes only one element from the heap.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Five operations would remove only half of the elements when each operation removes one element.
explanations.c: Correct. Ten elements require ten root-removal operations when exactly one element is removed per operation.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Removing one element per operation does not require two operations per element.

questions.question: 3. After removing the root from a binary heap, which element is typically moved to the root position before the heap property is restored?

answers.a: The last element in the heap
answers.c: The left child of the root

explanations.a: Correct. The last element is moved to the root position, and the heap property is then restored by adjusting it downward as needed.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Heap removal does not select a leaf based on its value in this way.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The left child is not necessarily the appropriate replacement for the removed root.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Heap removal does not identify the median as the replacement element.

questions.question: 4. In a max-heap, which element is obtained when the root is removed?

explanations.a: Incorrect. The root of a max-heap is not selected according to the minimum value.
explanations.b: Correct. The maximum element is at the root of a max-heap, so removing the root removes the maximum element.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The heap property does not place the median element at the root.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The root is determined by the max-heap property rather than being arbitrary.

questions.question: 5. What is the purpose of restoring the heap property after removing the root?

answers.a: To make the array sorted in alphabetical order
answers.b: To ensure every element becomes unique
answers.c: To reduce the number of elements by half
answers.d: To ensure the remaining elements satisfy the heap-order condition

explanations.a: Incorrect. Heap restoration is based on key comparisons, not alphabetical ordering.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Restoring the heap property does not modify values to make them unique.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Heap restoration changes the arrangement of elements but does not generally halve the heap size.
explanations.d: Correct. Restoration rearranges the affected elements so that the heap-order condition holds throughout the remaining heap.

questions.question: 6. If a heap contains $n$ elements, what is the height of the heap in terms of $n$?

explanations.a: Incorrect. A binary heap can have more than one level when $n$ grows.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The height of a complete binary tree grows much more slowly than the number of nodes.
explanations.c: Correct. A binary heap is a complete binary tree, whose height is $O(\log n)$.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The height does not grow quadratically with the number of elements.

questions.question: 7. During repeated root removals in Heap Sort with a max-heap, where is the removed maximum element placed in the array?

answers.a: At the beginning of the array
answers.b: At the end of the current unsorted portion

explanations.a: Incorrect. Placing each extracted maximum at the beginning would not match the usual in-place Heap Sort arrangement.
explanations.b: Correct. The extracted maximum is placed at the end of the current unsorted portion, where it remains in its final sorted position.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Heap Sort uses a deliberate position for each extracted element rather than a random location.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The standard in-place procedure does not require a separate linked list.

questions.question: 8. Which heap operation is primarily used to restore a heap after its root has been replaced?

explanations.a: Correct. After the root is replaced, heapify-down compares the replacement with its children and moves it downward until the heap property is restored.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Linear search locates values but does not restore the structural heap-order condition.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Binary search requires a sorted sequence and is not the operation used to repair a heap.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Insertion sort is a sorting algorithm, not the local repair operation used after root replacement.

questions.question: 9. If each root removal from a binary heap takes $O(\log n)$ time and $n$ elements are removed, what is the overall order of the repeated removals?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Multiplying the cost of one logarithmic-time removal by $n$ removals gives a larger bound than linear time.
explanations.b: Incorrect. This is the cost associated with a single heap adjustment, not all $n$ removals.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A logarithmic-time adjustment repeated $n$ times does not produce a quadratic bound.
explanations.d: Correct. Performing $n$ removals at $O(\log n)$ each gives $O(n\log n)$ total work, ignoring the small change in heap size.
